name: Detox teas / juice cleanses

lead: Detox teas and juice cleanses are taken for reduced bloating, a leaner face and midsection, and clearer skin, with the promise of flushing out toxins.

Many teas work as laxatives or diuretics, so people commonly report short-term drops on the scale and less bloat from lost water and gut contents. Published reviews have found no compelling evidence that detox diets remove toxins or help weight beyond short-term loss that is regained, and skin effects are untested.

paras: People drink teas daily for a set number of days, or replace meals with juices for one to several days. They are often used before an event or as a kickstart to a diet.

Prolonged fasting can be dangerous, and a kidney injury case was linked to a green-smoothie cleanse. Laxative and diuretic ingredients can cause cramps, dehydration and electrolyte loss. Belief in detox can also delay medical care.

angle.text: Users take detox teas and juice cleanses for a leaner face, less bloating and clearer skin. Laxative or diuretic effects cut water weight and bloat, so short-term scale and midsection changes are commonly reported. Reviews do not support the claim of removing toxins, and skin effects are untested.

lead: Detox teas and juice cleanses are consumer products and short-term diets marketed as ways to remove unspecified "toxins" from the body. They are part of the wider alternative-medicine category of detoxification, which also includes fasting, colon cleansing and restricted diets [1]. In appearance-focused communities they are discussed mainly in connection with clearer skin, a leaner face and reduced bloating.

Proponents say that modern food and the environment leave contaminants that accumulate in the body and that a cleanse helps release them [1][2]. Published reviews have found no compelling evidence that detox diets remove toxins or aid weight management, and a 2015 critical review in the Journal of Human Nutrition and Dietetics called for independent regulatory review of such products [1].
infobox: Herbal teas, juice-only diets, restricted-food regimens

paras: Detoxification in the alternative-medicine sense aims to remove unspecified toxins said to build up in the body. Common forms include dieting, fasting, eating only certain foods, colon cleansing, chelation and some intravenous therapies [1]. Detox diets may limit intake to water or juice, remove fats or highly processed foods, or emphasise fibre [1].
Detox teas are herbal blends sold with similar promises. The reference material used for this article does not describe their ingredients or regulation in detail.

By the 19th century the theory of autointoxication, in which constipation was thought to produce toxins that are reabsorbed, had gained support, and it fell out of favour in the early 20th century. Walter Alvarez's 1919 JAMA article on so-called autointoxication symptoms is often cited as a turning point [1].

Interest returned with the growth of alternative medicine in the 1970s [1]. Juice-based cleansing drew on figures such as Norman Walker, who built an early juicer in 1936, and Jay Kordich in the 1990s [2].

A 2015 critical review by Klein and Kiat found no compelling evidence that detox diets manage weight or eliminate toxins [1]. A 2017 review by Obert and colleagues reported that strict calorie restriction can cause short-term weight loss that is regained when normal eating resumes [1].

Clinicians and dietitians' bodies cited in the literature state that the liver and kidneys already handle most ingested toxins [1]. The British Dietetic Association has described the idea as a marketing myth [1].

Prolonged fasting recommended by some detox regimens can be dangerous, whereas a single short fast is considered unlikely to cause harm [1]. A 2018 report in the American Journal of Kidney Diseases linked a green-smoothie cleanse to acute oxalate nephropathy [1].
Commentators also note that belief in detox can delay effective treatment of disease, and describe individual cases of serious harm reported in news media [1].
No studies found on detox teas specifically for appearance outcomes. Reviews of detox diets more broadly are summarised above [1].

timeline.event: Walter Alvarez publishes an influential JAMA article questioning autointoxication symptoms [1].
Norman Walker designs an early mechanical juicer [2].
Klein and Kiat publish a critical review of detox diets [1].
